Detecting galamsey with satellite embeddings: the rs05 approach

How we build the labels, train the classifier, and prove it works — a plain-language companion to rs07_labels.R and rs05_embedding_classifier.R

Ghana galamsey project · Till Meissner

2026-07-15

1. What we are trying to do

We want a map of artisanal gold mining (galamsey) for every year 2017–2024, covering the south-west Ghana mining belt, built from satellite data. No such annual map exists: the best available dataset (Barenblitt et al. 2021) stops in 2019, and every other mining inventory is a one-off snapshot. The economic analysis in Part 2 of this project needs a panel — mining presence by location by year — and rs05 is the machine that produces it.

The output of rs05 is one probability raster per year (each 10 m pixel gets a score “how mine-like does this pixel look this year?”). A later step (rs07_embedding_panel) thresholds those into binary mine/no-mine maps and aggregates them to the hex panel.

The whole approach stands on three legs, each covered below:

  1. Features — what the classifier looks at (AlphaEarth satellite embeddings, §2)
  2. Labels — how it learns what a mine looks like (rs07_labels.R, §4–5)
  3. Validation — how we know whether to believe it (held-out SmallMinesDS + ablation, §7–8)

Why not just use the existing mining shapefiles?

Global mining inventories already exist — Maus et al. (2022) and Tang & Werner (2023) both ship Ghana polygons. Why build a classifier at all? The one-sentence answer: they tell you where mining ever was (as of ~2019–22); this pipeline tells you where it was each year — and the economic analysis runs on the “each year”.

Maus / Tang & Werner shapefiles This pipeline
Time dimension One snapshot (Maus: 2019; Tang: undocumented mix ~2019–22) Annual maps 2017–2024 → onset years, entry dynamics, stocks & flows
Artisanal vs industrial No usable type attribute in Ghana (checked: Tang’s commodity field is placemark junk there; Maus has no split) Learns the artisanal class from Barenblitt’s minetype flag
ASM coverage Openly incomplete: Tang mapped ASM “case-study only”; Maus drew inside 10 km buffers of an industrial-mine registry Generalises from the signature of mining — finds small riverine galamsey the inventories missed
Accuracy Tang: no formal assessment at all; Maus: assessed, but not for ASM Quantified against an independent expert test set (OA 84–88 %, PA/UA per model — §7–8)
Consistency over time Splicing inventories confounds real change with differing mapping definitions Same features, same model, every year — year-over-year change is meaningful
Treatment intensity Polygon in/out only Continuous probabilities → mined area per hex-year, dose–response designs

The time dimension is the decisive row: event studies and Callaway–Sant’Anna cohorts need a treatment clock — when did mining start here? — and a cross-sectional shapefile cannot supply one at any price. Everything else is a real but secondary bonus.

And it isn’t “our approach versus theirs”: Maus and Tang are inside the pipeline as training labels (§4). If the research question were merely “where has Ghana ever had mining, roughly as of 2020?”, the shapefiles would suffice and this pipeline would be over-engineering. It’s the panel dimension the analysis lives on that they cannot provide.

2. The features: AlphaEarth satellite embeddings

The classical remote-sensing route is to download raw imagery, fight through cloud masking (SW Ghana averages ~83 % cloud cover), compute hand-picked spectral indices (NDVI, NDWI, bare-soil…), and hope those indices capture what distinguishes a mine. We skip most of that by using Google’s AlphaEarth embeddings (Brown et al. 2025; GOOGLE/SATELLITE_EMBEDDING/V1/ANNUAL in Earth Engine).

An embedding is a 64-number summary of everything the satellites saw at one 10 m pixel over one calendar year — Sentinel-2 optical, Sentinel-1 radar (which sees through cloud), thermal, climate, terrain — compressed by a neural network that Google trained globally. Think of each pixel getting a 64-dimensional “fingerprint” of its annual appearance and dynamics:

  • pixels that look/behave alike (two mining ponds; two cocoa farms) get similar fingerprints — the vectors are unit-length, so similarity is simply a dot product (cosine similarity);
  • the fingerprints are consistent across years, so a classifier trained on 2019 can be applied to any year 2017–2024;
  • cloud robustness, multi-sensor fusion, and temporal aggregation are already baked in.

Our job reduces to something much smaller and more tractable: teach a simple classifier which fingerprints mean “galamsey”. We use a random forest (200 trees) on the 64 bands — with features this strong the choice of classifier is secondary (Brown et al.’s own benchmarks show shallow models all perform similarly on these embeddings).

The catch: embeddings exist only from 2017. Anything earlier belongs to a separate Landsat-based phase (see §9).

4. Getting to the labels (rs07_labels.R)

No single ground-truth dataset is good enough on its own, so we harmonise three positive sources and hold a fourth back as the referee:

Source What it is Coverage / vintage Known weaknesses
Barenblitt et al. 2021 Random-forest mining map from Landsat, the only source with an artisanal/industrial split SW Ghana, 2019 extent (+ 2007–17 series) Producer accuracy 75.6 % → misses ~1 in 4 mines; itself a model output
Maus et al. 2022 (v2) Hand-drawn “mining lands” polygons around known sites, global Ghana subset (577 polygons), drawn on the 2019 Sentinel-2 mosaic Broad definition (includes non-mine islands); 54.5 % of its validation errors sit < 50 m from polygon borders
Tang & Werner 2023 Hand-drawn mine-feature contours on 0.15–10 m Google Earth imagery, global Ghana subset (1,907 polygons), mixed vintage ≈ 2019–2022 No formal accuracy assessment; positional RMSE 39.7 m; commodity attribute unusable in Ghana
SmallMinesDS (Ofori-Ampofo et al. 2025) Dense expert ASGM masks, 10 m, two dated epochs 5 SW districts, Jan 2016 + Jan 2022 Held out — used only for validation (§7)

The two geometric moves

Polygon borders are where all these datasets are least trustworthy (digitising slop, positional error, mixed pixels). And absence of a polygon never means “no mining” — every source has known omissions. rs07 turns both problems into geometry:

  1. Erode inward. Training positives are sampled only from the polygon core: Maus shrunk by 50 m, Tang by 40 m (matching their measured error scales), Barenblitt kept as-is (its 30 m Landsat pixels are already coarse). Small sites that vanish under erosion — exactly the riverine galamsey shape we care about — are salvaged as a single interior point each (185 of them), rather than being lost.
  2. Buffer outward. The union of all raw footprints from all sources (including industrial mines and every SmallMinesDS patch) plus a 1 km buffer becomes the exclusion mask (~11,000 km², 4.6 % of Ghana). Negatives — examples of “not a mine” — are sampled only outside it. So a spot may only teach the model “this is what no-mining looks like” if no dataset we have places mining anywhere near it.

The result: 9,690 positive polygons + 185 salvage points, each carrying its source and vintage. The full label set over Ghana (interactive version: outputs/figures/labels/labels_overview_map.html):

5. Vintage matching: labels must meet the right year

The label sources are snapshots from different moments, and galamsey moves fast — a 2019 polygon may be forest in 2017 and abandoned by 2022. Training a “2019 polygon” against a 2022 embedding would teach the model nonsense. So every source is paired with the embedding year that matches when its imagery was actually taken:

  • Barenblitt & Maus → 2019 embeddings (both are 2019 snapshots);
  • Tang & Werner → 2021 embeddings (drawn on whatever Google Earth imagery was freshest, ≈ 2019–2022; 2021 is the midpoint);
  • SmallMinesDS Jan-2022 masks → score predictions made on 2022 embeddings; the Jan-2016 epoch predates the embeddings entirely and is reserved for the Landsat phase.

This is a point the SmallMinesDS paper makes explicitly: it criticises Maus and Tang & Werner by name for lacking acquisition dates, “prohibiting their use as labels for machine learning”. Vintage-pairing is our answer to that critique.

6. Training (rs05_embedding_classifier.R)

With labels and features in place, training is deliberately simple:

Ingredient Choice Why
Positive pixels 2,000 Barenblitt + 1,000 Maus + 1,000 Tang Barenblitt weighted up: it alone defines the artisanal target class
Negative pixels 3 × positives, per vintage year, outside the exclusion mask Class imbalance under control; negatives drawn from the same years as the positives they oppose
Sampling Pixel locations drawn locally in R (area-weighted inside the label cores; negatives rejection-sampled outside the exclusion mask, max one point per 10 m pixel), then Earth Engine reads the embedding bands at those points Keeps all geometry work where we control it exactly — and sending polygons to EE embeds their GeoJSON in every request, breaking the 10 MB payload limit. Study area = convex hull of Barenblitt positives + 10 km
Classifier Random forest, 200 trees, on the 64 embedding bands Strong-features/simple-model; probability output mode for the maps
Bookkeeping Every training point keeps source + vintage properties Enables the ablation (§8) and later spatial cross-validation

The trained model is then applied to each year’s embedding mosaic, 2017–2024, producing eight probability maps.

7. Validation: how we know whether to believe it

Why SmallMinesDS is the referee

Validating against your own training sources proves nothing (the pond-detection prototype had exactly this circularity problem). SmallMinesDS is kept strictly out of training and makes a good referee because its errors are plausibly uncorrelated with ours:

  • different annotators and workflow (mean-shift segmentation + two cross-validating experts + per-block RF assist with human correction — independent of Barenblitt);
  • different feature stack (Sentinel-2 + Sentinel-1 + DEM at patch level, not AlphaEarth);
  • precisely dated (January 2022), so we know which embedding year it can judge.

From masks to a test set

rs07 §12 converts the 2,135 held-out 2022 mask patches into point labels a GEE error matrix can consume: per patch, up to 5 core mining pixels and up to 2 core non-mining pixels — “core” meaning a 3×3 neighbourhood erosion per class, so no test point sits on a mask edge (mixed 10 m pixels). Both classes are then downsampled to the minority count, giving a balanced test set of 4,270 mining + 4,270 non-mining points. Balance matters: on a wildly imbalanced test set, overall accuracy rewards models that just say “no mine” everywhere.

The numbers we report

For each model, the SmallMinesDS-2022 error matrix yields:

Metric Plain-language meaning
OA (overall accuracy) share of all test points classified correctly
kappa accuracy above what chance agreement would give
mine PA (producer’s acc. / recall) of the true mines, how many did we find? — misses = omission
mine UA (user’s acc. / precision) of the pixels we call mine, how many really are? — false alarms = commission

PA and UA are the pair to watch: a model can trivially max one at the other’s expense. The script also prints an in-sample 80/20 split accuracy — ignore it except as a sanity check; a random split leaks spatial structure and is always optimistic. The honest number is the SmallMinesDS row.

8. The ablation: which labels actually help?

Because every training point is tagged with its source, we can train the same RF on different label subsets and score each against the same held-out test set. One table answers several standing questions at once (outputs/tables/rs05_ablation_smallminesds2022.csv):

Row Trains on The question it answers
barenblitt Barenblitt only How far does the (model-derived) backbone alone go?
maus / tang one hand-drawn source Is either human inventory sufficient by itself?
human Maus + Tang Can we drop Barenblitt entirely — killing the circularity worry that we inherit its systematic errors?
all all three Does combining beat the best single source? (the default final model)
sim_mean_* — (one-class) Baseline: cosine similarity to the mean positive fingerprint — the original GEE “pond script” method, at three thresholds
sim_max_* — (one-class) Baseline: per-pixel max similarity over ~100 randomly chosen positive “prototypes” — the pond script’s v3, effectively nearest-neighbour matching

The similarity baselines matter for an honest comparison with the earlier prototype work: they use no negatives at all — just “does this pixel resemble known mines?” If the RF can’t clearly beat them on SmallMinesDS, the extra machinery isn’t earning its keep. (One subtlety: sim_max thresholds are calibrated on positives that are not prototypes, because a prototype matches itself with similarity ≈ 1.0 and would corrupt its own calibration.)

Decision rule: keep Barenblitt as training backbone unless the ablation shows human ≥ all on mine PA/UA — i.e. the circularity concern is settled empirically, not by argument.

9. Honest limitations

  • Circularity risk. Barenblitt is itself a classifier output; training on it can inherit its systematic errors. Mitigations: the erosion step, the independent referee, and the ablation’s human row as an explicit test.
  • The exclusion mask is not clean. All sources have known omission (Maus PA ≈ 79 %, ASM under-sampled), so “outside the mask” still contains some unlabelled mining — some negatives are secretly positives. This biases the classifier towards missing mines, not inventing them.
  • SW Ghana only (for now). The study area is the labelled belt; the north is unlabelled, not mine-free. Scaling up means widening STUDY_BUFFER_KM or swapping in the national boundary — and accepting that no validation data exists up there.
  • Nothing before 2017. The embedding era starts 2017. The 1995/2000–2016 history is a separate planned phase (Landsat + CCDC/LandTrendr change detection), for which the SmallMinesDS Jan-2016 masks are being reserved as its validation set.
  • What a “mine” is differs by source. Maus draws broad “mining lands”, Tang draws tight feature contours, Barenblitt maps spectral conversion — the same site gets different footprints. Erosion narrows the gap but the definitions never fully align.
  • Licences. Maus and SmallMinesDS are CC-BY-SA (share-alike): fine for internal training/validation; check before redistributing derived label datasets.
  • Not yet run. As of 2026-07-15 the rewired rs05 script is written but awaits an interactive GEE run (ee_Authenticate() blocks on a browser login), so the ablation table and probability maps don’t exist yet.
